procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order, dated May 19, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench) at Lucknow in Criminal Appeal No, 118 of 1967 and capital sentence No. 11 of 1967.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Allahabad High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences passed by the Sessions Judge, Hardoi.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court by special leave after the Allahabad High Court confirmed their convictions and sentences.

directions: The sentence of death imposed on the four appellants is set aside and the sentence of rigorous imprisonment for life is imposed on them.

issue.issue_text: Whether an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act for the non-examination of two independent eye-witnesses.

facts: The prosecution's case was primarily based on the testimony of four eyewitnesses who were family members of the two murder victims.
Two other independent eyewitnesses, Parsadi and Paragu, were mentioned but not examined by the prosecution.
The prosecution's explanation for not examining them was simply that they were 'not necessary witnesses'.
The defense did not challenge this explanation during the trial by cross-examining other witnesses or the Investigating Officer to find out why these two were considered unnecessary.
law: Under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act, a court may draw an adverse inference if a party withholds evidence that it could have produced.
A prosecutor is not obligated to examine every single witness, especially when many are available. They can make a selection, but this selection must be fair and honest.
An adverse inference can be drawn if it is shown that the prosecution deliberately kept witnesses away because their testimony would be inconvenient or unfavorable to its case.
application: The Court noted that while the prosecution's explanation that the witnesses were 'not necessary' was not very detailed, the defense accepted it at the time by not asking any follow-up questions.
The Court found nothing in the evidence to suggest that the witnesses were deliberately withheld for any 'oblique motive' or because they would have given testimony unfavorable to the prosecution.
Since the defense did not probe the issue at trial and there was no evidence of deliberate suppression, the Court found no basis to conclude that the non-examination was done for dishonest reasons.
The Court, therefore, agreed with the High Court's assessment that it was not possible to say the prosecution had deliberately withheld these two witnesses.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and refused to draw an adverse inference against the prosecution. The Court reasoned that the defense had not challenged the prosecution's explanation for the non-examination during the trial, and there was no evidence to suggest that the witnesses were deliberately withheld because their testimony would have been unfavorable to the prosecution's case.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a delay in sending the special report to the Magistrate, thereby casting doubt on the prosecution's case.

facts: The defense argued that there was a delay because the Magistrate at Hardoi testified to receiving the special report about the incident on June 6, 1966.
The defense contended that if the incident occurred and the report was sent on the evening of June 5th, the Magistrate should have received it that same night, not the next day.
application: The Court noted that the Magistrate's own testimony weakened the defense's argument. The Magistrate admitted he had not noted the time of receipt on June 6th.

The Magistrate also admitted he could not be certain he was in Hardoi on June 5th, as it was a Sunday, and acknowledged it was possible his peon received the report on the evening of the 5th and simply placed it before him on the morning of the 6th.
The Court found the controversy was definitively settled by the evidence of the Head Constable, P.W. 13.
P.W. 13 testified that he had sent a constable with the special report to the Magistrate at 7:30 P.M. on June 5th.
The same constable returned to the police station at 9:30 P.M. that same night after delivering the report, and this fact was officially recorded in a document (Ext. Ka-6).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that there was a delay. The evidence from the Head Constable and the official record (Ext. Ka-6) established that the special report was sent and delivered to the Magistrate on the night of the incident, June 5th. The Magistrate's notation of receiving it on June 6th was explained by the possibility of his peon receiving it the prior evening. Therefore, the timing of the report did not cast any doubt on the prosecution's case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act for the non-examination of two independent eye-witnesses.
appellant_arguments: Independent eye-witnesses (Parsadi and Paragu) were available but were purposely excluded, and only family members of the deceased were examined.
The prosecution's explanation that these two witnesses were 'not necessary' was unsatisfactory, as noted by the High Court which stated it would have been better if they had been examined.
The High Court erred by refusing to draw an adverse inference against the prosecution under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act.
Citing case law (Habeeb Mohammed v. State of Hyderabad), it is the prosecution's duty to examine material witnesses, and withholding them casts serious reflection on the fairness of the trial.
Citing another case (Darya Singh v. State of Punjab), a prosecutor should not keep back eyewitnesses just because their evidence might be unfavorable.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution provided an explanation that the two independent eye-witnesses were not necessary.
The defense did not challenge this explanation during the trial by questioning other witnesses on the matter.
There is no evidence to suggest that the witnesses were withheld because they would have given unfavorable testimony ('turned out to be inconvenient witnesses').

cases.case_name: Kirpal Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.principle: The Supreme Court will not normally review evidence and interfere with concurrent findings of fact unless it is shown that the trial was vitiated by some illegality or irregularity of procedure, was held contrary to the rules of natural justice, or the judgment resulted in a gross miscarriage of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When numerous eyewitnesses are available, the prosecution has the discretion to select which witnesses to examine, but this selection must be fair, honest, and not for the purpose of suppressing inconvenient witnesses; an adverse inference against the prosecution for non-production of a witness can only be drawn if it is shown that the witness was withheld because their testimony would have been unfavorable to the prosecution's case. Additionally, in cases of group liability for murder where the evidence does not establish who inflicted the fatal blows, all participants armed with equally dangerous weapons should receive the same punishment.
obiter: The Supreme Court will not normally proceed to review concurrent findings of fact unless it is shown that the trial is vitiated by some illegality or irregularity of procedure, that it was held in a manner contrary to rules of natural justice, or that the judgment under appeal has resulted in a gross miscarriage of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that no adverse inference could be drawn against the prosecution for not examining two independent eye-witnesses. The prosecutor has the discretion to select witnesses, especially when many are available, provided the selection is fair and not intended to suppress inconvenient evidence. Since the defense did not challenge the prosecution's explanation at trial and there was no evidence to suggest the witnesses were deliberately withheld for an oblique motive, the High Court was correct in its refusal to draw an adverse inference.
legal_tests_applied: In a case where a large number of persons have witnessed an incident, it is open to the prosecutor to make a selection of witnesses to examine.
The selection of witnesses by the prosecution must be fair and honest and not with a view to suppress inconvenient witnesses.
To draw an adverse inference under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act, it must be shown that persons who had witnessed the incident have been deliberately kept back.
The failure to examine material witnesses, if shown to be a deliberate act of withholding, can constitute a serious infirmity in the proof of the prosecution's case.
why_appellant_lost: The defense remained content with the prosecution's explanation at trial that the two independent eye-witnesses were 'not necessary' and did not question other witnesses to challenge this explanation.
There was nothing in the evidence to suggest that the witnesses were not produced because they would have turned out to be inconvenient witnesses.
The appellant failed to demonstrate that the prosecution had deliberately withheld the two witnesses for any oblique motive, which is a necessary condition for drawing an adverse inference.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution provided an explanation for the non-examination of the two witnesses, stating they were not necessary.
The defense's failure to challenge the prosecution's explanation at trial lent it credence.
The record was devoid of any evidence suggesting the prosecution's motive was to suppress unfavorable testimony.
policy_considerations: The duty of the prosecutor is to assist the Court in reaching a proper conclusion, not merely to secure a conviction.
A prosecutor should never adopt the device of keeping back eye-witnesses only because their evidence is likely to go against the prosecution.
Withholding a material witness from the court can cast a serious reflection on the fairness of the trial.
